extracted.intended_audience: vehicle manufacturers, test laboratories, compliance engineers, and safety regulators involved with FMVSS No. 210 anchorage strength testing
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory specification and evaluation criteria for the Force Application Devices (FAD1 and FAD2) and the associated FMVSS No. 210 anchorage strength test procedures, including device design, drawings, positioning, attachments, and repeatability requirements. Intended to guide manufacturers and test labs in fabricating and using the FADs and in interpreting the test protocol.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dimensions of the FADs
rubrics_metrics.description: The NPRM included dimensions of the FAD1 and FAD2 and compared them to Hybrid III ATDs; the FAD1's dimensions most closely resembled the 50th percentile adult male and the FAD2's dimensions were less than that of the 10-year-old child test dummy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FAD2 was developed as a scaled-down FAD1 (not modeled after a particular Hybrid III ATD or occupant category); shoulder pivot height, shoulder breadth, and hip breadth are 60%, 71%, and 66% of the 50th percentile male respectively. The weight of the FADs cannot be used to infer representation of a particular ATD because FADs lack lower legs, arms, and heads. The intent is to assess seat belt anchorage performance, not occupant crash forces; manufacturers may certify using body blocks if concerned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical placement / handling considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledges that placing FADs in and out of the vehicle depends on technician strength and lab policies; test labs may have lifting limits that affect who can place FADs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NHTSA notes similar handling issues exist for ATD dummies (e.g., HIII 50th male ~170 lb). If laboratory policies or practical constraints impede use of FADs, manufacturers may opt to certify using the current body blocks.

rubrics_metrics.name: FAD abdomen/pelvic area and hip clip design
rubrics_metrics.description: FAD pelvic area includes a molded protrusion to facilitate lap belt placement; original aluminum connecting pieces damaged belt webbing leading to the development of hip clips. Initial hip clips caused belt breakage and were redesigned with smoother edges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Redesigned hip clips are intended to prevent webbing damage and improve pelvic/torso biofidelity; prototype tests with redesigned hip clips showed no belt damage. The hip clip drawings in the proposal were further modified (angled to prevent belt ride-up, stronger and bigger hardware). Agency believes a pivot between torso and pelvis is necessary to properly position the FAD; manufacturers' concerns about non-perfect biofidelity are acknowledged but testing supports redesign efficacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of torso–pelvis pivot
rubrics_metrics.description: The agency believes a pivot point between the torso and pelvis portions is necessary to properly position the FAD in the seat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different seat designs and seat contours require the ability to pivot torso and pelvis to properly position the device; removal of pivot would risk improper seating and reduced repeatability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bridged pull yoke definition and interaction with seat cushion
rubrics_metrics.description: The bridged pull yoke 'bridges the torso and pelvis on the FAD1 or FAD2 to apply the required force to a Type 1 seat belt assembly.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concern that bridged pull yoke could dig into soft seat cushions was investigated; indicant tests did not show consistent evidence of digging or interference. Agency declined to redesign the bridged pull yoke. If interference occurs in a particular test, pull angle or chain adjustments may alleviate it; manufacturers may elect to certify using body block option.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attachment points for force actuator (Type 1 vs Type 2 belts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the force actuator attaches to the FAD depends on seat belt type: for Type 2 belts, actuator connects to separate connection points on torso (via torso pull yoke/eye bolt) and pelvis (through hole); for Type 1 belts, actuator connects to a bridged pull yoke which attaches to the torso and pelvis attachment points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory text and drawings were modified to use the same part names as the design drawings (e.g., 'eye bolt') and to clarify attachment points. NHTSA does not specify exactly how the actuator is attached (e.g., chain choice) because laboratory equipment can vary and some labs test to failure while others test to FMVSS performance requirements. This mirrors the current body block specification which likewise does not prescribe exact actuator attachments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and incorporation of design drawings and 3-D data
rubrics_metrics.description: 2‑D design drawings for FAD1 and FAD2 are docketed and incorporated by reference; 3‑D CAD files could not be docketed but 3‑D solid models are being provided as supplemental reference materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NHTSA provided scanned 3‑D solid models as supplemental documentation (not incorporated by reference into 49 CFR 571.5) and made them available via NHTSA's FTP site to facilitate fabrication. Minor dimensional changes were made to some drawings to match scanned models; hip clip drawings were modified to reflect redesign. Agency believes the drawing package is sufficiently detailed for fabrication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Missing tolerance values in drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments noted the drawing packages were incomplete due to lack of tolerance designations in numerous places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NHTSA added tolerances to all dimensions specified in the finalized drawing package; if a tolerance is not indicated next to a dimension, an overall tolerance summary is specified at the bottom of the drawing page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-form design advantages
rubrics_metrics.description: NPRM stated advantages of the FAD over body blocks: more representative human form, does not put unrealistic bending force on belt buckle, lacks sharp edges reducing likelihood of belt breakage, reduces seat belt spool-out, easier and quicker to position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency clarified that human-form advantages reduce problematic interactions between device and belt/vehicle and could allow testing of unconventional seat belt geometries (four- and five-point belts). Primary advantages are ease and repeatability of testing. Although FMVSS No. 210 addresses anchorages not belt assemblies, NHTSA prefers using the vehicle's original belt assembly for simplicity when possible; shorter substitute belts or cables may be used where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect on seat back deformation (interaction with seat structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concern that FAD could reinforce seat structure (especially integrated seats) and yield different deformation than body blocks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency research tests show the FAD pulls away from the seat back during testing and does not reinforce the seat structure; FAD geometry (hinges at the H-point, not two independent blocks) better represents occupant dynamics. Commenters did not provide supporting data; agency stands by test observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positioning procedure — seat reference plane and seat adjustment
rubrics_metrics.description: Final rule defines 'seat reference plane' as 'the vertical plane that passes through the SgRP and is parallel to the direction that the seat faces' and requires aligning the FAD midsagittal plane with that plane; seat adjustment to the rearmost normal riding or driving position as specified by the manufacturer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This replaces inconsistent NPRM terminology and aligns seat adjustment provisions with the manufacturer's SgRP so tests are consistent with body block zone references. The rule adds an FAD-specific definition of 'midsagittal plane.' The rearmost normal riding/driving position includes all seat adjustments (horizontal, vertical, seat back angle, cushion angle) as specified by the manufacturer; OVSC typically requests this information prior to testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection procedure for FAD1 vs FAD2 and adjacency/contact rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed iterative procedure: place FAD1s on each seat and, if prior to conducting the test there is contact between FAD1s or they cannot be positioned side-by-side due to contact, replace an inboard FAD1 with an FAD2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency will not allow adjacent FADs to contact each other at the onset of testing (when positioned prior to preload). Contact between adjacent FADs once preloads have begun is not prohibited (incidental contact during preload/loading is allowed if it does not unduly influence results). Contact with vehicle interior is permissible if it does not interfere with loading or attaining required load; normally tests are conducted with doors removed for outboard seats. Manufacturers may choose body blocks if concerned about contact effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact definition and procedural clarifications (what constitutes 'contact')
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments questioned whether 'contact' meant any touching or only contact that interferes with functionality/independent operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency clarified that any contact between adjacent FADs is prohibited at initial positioning; incidental contact during preload/loading is permissible. For vehicle interior contact, permissible only if it does not affect loading or achieving required loads; left to case-by-case determination and laboratory test procedures may address specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of FAD2 on buses and heavy-duty trucks
rubrics_metrics.description: FAD2 was developed for designated seating positions too narrow to accommodate FAD1; commenters asked to mandate FAD2 for double seats in coaches or alter FAD1 size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency declines to mandate FAD2-only testing for buses; prefers objective protocol for when to replace FAD1 with FAD2. Does not change FAD1 size. Testing showed no failures with either FAD; design margins expected to accommodate slight force vector differences. Heavy-duty manufacturers may use body blocks if FAD1 does not fit or they are uncomfortable certifying with FAD2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bottoming out of hydraulic cylinders
rubrics_metrics.description: NPRM stated the FAD would eliminate hydraulic cylinder bottoming out sometimes occurring with current body blocks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency conducted FAD tests on air suspension seats in heavy vehicles with no indication of increased cylinder travel or bottoming out. Agency believes current body blocks have greater range of motion and are more likely to cause cylinders to reach the end of stroke than the FAD.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeatability of seating and applied forces
rubrics_metrics.description: NHTSA assessed repeatability by (1) multiple technicians positioning FAD1s in nine vehicles and measuring placement with a Faro Arm and (2) testing repeatability of forces applied to anchorages using multiple tests and load cells.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seating consistency: of 27 positionings (3 technicians × 9 vehicles), average variance for positioning was less than 1/4 inch—acceptable and within FMVSS No. 208 H-point tolerance (12.7 mm / 1/2 inch). Forces: analyses (coefficient of variation, general linear model, mixed model) indicated repeatable loads across channels; most channels rated 'excellent,' with one 'good' and one 'acceptable' (the latter had higher measurement error but small mean scale relative to primary belt load). NHTSA concludes FADs produce sufficiently repeatable results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming consistency between regulatory text and drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed regulatory text did not clearly identify where forces are to be applied using consistent part names; commenters requested clearer labeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NHTSA modified regulatory text to use the same part names used in the design drawings (e.g., 'eye bolt') and added clarifying bridged pull yoke drawings (NHTSA221-210-27 and NHTSA221-210-27J) to the finalized drawing package to clarify attachment points for torso, pelvis, and actuator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Option to use body blocks instead of FADs
rubrics_metrics.description: Throughout comments and responses, agency notes manufacturers can choose to certify compliance using the current body blocks as an alternative to the FADs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This option is repeatedly emphasized where manufacturers express concerns about fit, contact, possible interference, or uncertainties about test equivalence; it serves as a compliance alternative when FADs are impractical or yield concerns in particular vehicles.
